A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Scaling Small Agents Through Strategy Auctions. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and match reliably across additions, relocations, and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original HST-Bench evaluations, routing comparisons, ablations, statistical tests, and qualitative analyses of agent behavior.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds memory-pruning experiments, human jury validation, timing measurements, tool-cost simulations, and cross-family auction analyses.

M1.justification: The principal SALE procedure is retained. Appendix D.5 implements a previously prospective extension by adding a tool-latency penalty to the routing cost. Appendix M.2 also introduces a configuration where additional agents bid but the original Qwen3 jury remains fixed. The clarified entropy calculation and scoring scale already appeared in v1's appendices.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same HST-Bench deep-search and coding coverage, source datasets, and complexity ranges. Added studies reuse its tasks or generated plans. Different model families, memory subsets, and synthetic cost penalties change experimental configurations rather than the represented benchmark tasks.

E2.justification: The evaluated routing comparators remain the best single agent, WTP, CARROT, TO-Router, FrugalGPT, and the oracle analysis. The additional Gemma, Llama, and Ministral agents are auction participants or subjects of signal comparisons, not newly evaluated competing routing methods.

E3.justification: The main evaluation protocol is retained, but v2 substantially expands experimental designs. Additions include 100-task tool-penalty and timing studies, leave-one-out memory experiments with specified bank sizes and retention windows, and blinded ratings of 100 plans. Appendix M evaluates Gemma 3 with newly fitted weights and a mixed pool with frozen Qwen3 weights and an unchanged jury.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and error analyses, v2 adds tests of memory-size and retention-window sensitivity, jury alignment with human judgments and downstream success, tool-cost sensitivity, measured auction overhead, and cross-family transfer. These examine several previously untested questions about the mechanism's reliability and practical applicability.

E5.justification: The original five task-order permutations, standard deviations, t-tests, and bootstrap confidence intervals remain unchanged. Appendix I.3 adds five sampling seeds per memory size and reports seed-level variability. Appendix J.2 adds point-biserial correlation testing. This does not establish an increase in runs for the original benchmark results.

E6.justification: Table 1's benchmark scores are unchanged, but substantial diagnostic results are added: 3.59-second auction time, human-jury correlations of 0.74–0.82, memory-pruning outcomes, and cross-family allocations. The new tool-penalty sweep reduces 32B allocation from 23% to 11% within that experiment. Summary figures also change: largest-agent reliance reduction 53% to 52%, simple-task relative performance approximately 87% to 90%, and the deep-search savings range 33–53% to 36–53%. These are not improved same-setting benchmark scores.

T1.justification: Appendix D.5 adds a mathematical definition extending cost by beta times planned tool-call count times synthetic per-call latency. The original min–max MILP, Shapley formulation, and refinement equations remain unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the reported largest-agent reliance reduction from 53% to 52%, and the introduction revises simple-task relative performance from approximately 87% to 90%. The five principal contributions and conclusions about complexity, strategy-based routing, and small-agent improvement retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new evidence as supporting jury validity, pruning tolerance, and preliminary cross-family applicability. Its limitations now explicitly identify untested large memories, model-version changes, and task-distribution shifts. Tool-cost handling advances from future work to a preliminary demonstration, while broader impacts adds a specific explanation of how efficiency can increase the scale of harmful applications.

D1.justification: The timing study newly documents concurrent vLLM serving and eight H100 GPUs per node. Added experiments specify memory settings and whether auction weights are refitted or frozen. Existing prompts, decoding settings, retrieval configuration, and solver details are retained; moving entropy and scoring-scale explanations into the main text is not new disclosure.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature grounding for price–quality auctions, jury scoring, and Shapley analysis of auctions. It also replaces the references supporting order-sensitive evaluation with Fan et al. and StreamBench. The main positioning relative to routing and memory-based adaptation remains intact; numerous bibliographic updates concern existing works.

P1.justification: Local rewrites clarify scoring, limitations, and interpretation, alongside punctuation and terminology edits. New appendix subsections are integrated, and former Appendices J and K become K and L. The main narrative and section sequence remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 9, 11, and 23–26 using the existing presentation style. Original figures and benchmark displays are retained. Figure 9's misleading 'Smallest agent share' axis label becomes 'Share', Figure 5 gains explanatory caption text, and other changes mainly involve reflow and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens the evidence through direct human validation of jury scores, measured auction latency, and targeted sensitivity studies, while stating applicability limits more precisely. These improve confidence in the mechanism and its practicality. The gain is limited because the main benchmark evidence is unchanged and the new pruning and cross-family studies chiefly measure auction signals and allocations rather than downstream accuracy.
